title: Name days
hook: many Orthodox and Catholic Christians celebrate their saint's day

segments.voice: Yesterday, crosses of many lands: ringed, inked, woven, three-barred. Your line was many crosses. Did any cross's shape stop you this time? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-nine.

A phone buzzes before breakfast. Then again, and again. By lunch, a man named Nikos has a stack of messages, a call from his aunt, and a tray of pastries waiting at work. It isn't his birthday. Nobody's asking how old he is. It's his name day: the feast of Saint Nicholas, the saint he's named for. Tonight, friends may drop by without being invited, because on a name day, in his family, the door is open. In some Orthodox and Catholic families, a name day is celebrated as warmly as a birthday. Today: name days.

First, what a name day is. In Catholic and Orthodox life, saints are remembered on particular days of the year. If you're named for a saint, that saint's day becomes your day too. Some go to church that morning. Some families eat together. The idea underneath is that the saint is a companion, someone who walked the road before you. The letter to the Hebrews pictures the faithful who came before as a crowd in the stands: "we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses." A name day picks one face out of that cloud and says: this one is yours. Next, a naming in Luke's Gospel. Elizabeth has a son in her old age, and the neighbors want to call him Zacharias, after his father. Elizabeth says no, he'll be called John. They turn to Zacharias, who can't speak, and he asks for a writing tablet: "His name is John. And they marvelled all." The boy has a story attached to his name before he can say a word. And in John's Gospel, Jesus meets Simon and gives him a new name: "thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone." A name, and a calling with it. Then, a promise in Isaiah: "Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." Isaiah speaks those words to Israel, a whole people, and still the phrase is personal: called by name. Last, a strange line from the Bible's last book. In Revelation, the one who overcomes is given "a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it." A name known only to the one who receives it. Not every church keeps name days; other churches honor the saints in other ways. But the thread is the same: in this faith, your name has a story.
screen: `I HAVE CALLED THEE BY THY NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your name's saint. Settle, and breathe. Start with your own name. Who gave it to you? Do you know why? Is it a family name, a name from a story, a name from the Bible? Then ask whether a saint shares it, or shares part of it. If you know of one, bring them to mind. If you don't, make a note to look later. Some names have no saint, and they still have a story. If you pray, you can hear Isaiah's words, I have called thee by thy name, as spoken to you. If you don't, just sit with the name you've carried all your life. The bell holds the time.
screen: `I HAVE CALLED THEE BY THY NAME.`

segments.voice: Name days. The feast of the saint you're named for, kept by some Catholic and Orthodox Christians as a day of their own.
Your line: your name has a story. Today, ask someone you know how they got their name, and listen to the whole answer. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Some Orthodox and Catholic Christians celebrate the feast day of the saint they are named for, often with church in the morning, a family meal and visits from friends; in Orthodox tradition a child is often given a saint's name at baptism.

notes: Audit: 'God doesn't call people as a crowd only. He calls them by name' read Isaiah 43:1 as individual address; the verse is spoken to Jacob/Israel, so the teach now says so. 'A name only you and God know' tightened to the text ('known only to the one who receives it'). howItsDone softened.
Editor pass: Revelation 2:17 is no longer called a line 'at the end of the Bible'; it is from the Bible's last book.
Index hook says 'many Orthodox and Catholic Christians'; the lesson softens this to 'some' under the claims rule. Confirm.
Hook: Nikos and the feast of Saint Nicholas is an illustrative scene; no date given. 'Celebrated as warmly as a birthday' is limited to 'some families'.
'Orthodox Christians receive a saint's name at baptism' (howItsDone): confirm this is accurate across Orthodox churches.
'Not every church keeps name days; other churches honor the saints in other ways': deliberately unquantified; confirm fair to Protestant churches.
Elizabeth's 'old age' from Luke 1:7, 1:36; the neighbors' wish and her refusal paraphrase Luke 1:59–60; 'writing tablet' paraphrases KJV 'writing table'.
The practice reads Isaiah 43:1 (spoken to Israel) as words a listener can hear personally; confirm this devotional use is acceptable.
